info.bio:
Chicago es, junto con Blood, Sweat & Tears (BS&T), la banda más representativa de lo que se dio en llamar Jazz Rock. Se fundó en la ciudad de su mismo nombre, en 1967, aunque inicialmente se denominó Chicago Transit Authority, nombre que debieron recortar por problemas jurídicos con el ayuntamiento de la ciudad. El grupo aún permanece en activo en 2007.

La banda estuvo integrada, inicialmente, por Lee Loughnane (trompeta), James Pankow (trombón)

scenes.desc: Bitches Brew de Miles Davis (1969) combina ritmos soul e instrumentos de rock amplificados y da un impulso tremendo al progresivo americano; Uncle Meat de Zappa es la respuesta del rock. Chicago y su fusión de vientos jazz y guitarras, Insect Trust, Gil Scott-Heron (precursor del rap con su spoken word), Flock, It's A Beautiful Day y Joy Of Cooking, uno de los primeros grupos liderados por mujeres.

podcast.title: Distinction from Blood, Sweat & Tears
podcast.body: Chicago has consistently maintained a clear distinction between their sound and that of Blood, Sweat & Tears, asserting themselves as a "rock band with horns" rather than a jazz-rock band. "Chicago made and still makes, if you go to their website, a very clear distinction between their sound and that of blood, sweat and tears."

podcast.title: Evolution of Sound (70s vs. 80s)
podcast.body: The 1970s version of Chicago was known for being experimental and politically engaged, in contrast to their 1980s sound, which leaned heavily into easy listening and soft pop with songs like "Hard to Say, I'm Sorry." "The 80s Chicago very heavy on easy listening, soft pop, you know, songs like Hard to Say, I'm Sorry. The 70s version of Chicago was not afraid to be a little political."

xref.title: Joe Hill (1915) – Swedish IWW Songwriter, Coined "Pie in the Sky," Executed by Firing Squad; Father of the Modern Protest Song
xref.body: Joe Hill was a Swedish-born itinerant laborer and songwriter for the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW), a socialist union founded in Chicago in 1905 that organized logging, mining, farm, and factory workers. Hill is credited with coining the phrase "Pie in the Sky." He was arrested and charged with the murder of two people in Salt Lake City, subject to a major media trial, found guilty, and executed by firing squad on November 19, 1915. He is considered the father of the modern protest song and has many fans in the rock world, including Tom Morello of Rage Against the Machine, who has organized a memorial in Joe's name, performed his songs, and released songs about him. "You can draw a straight line from Rage Against the Machine right back to the 1910s and Joe Hill."

xref.title: Ed Sanders' "Punk Rock" Usage (1970)
xref.body: The founder of The Fugs, Ed Sanders, described his 1970 solo album, "Sanders Truck Stop," as "punk rock redneck sentimentality" in a Chicago Tribune interview, marking one of the earliest uses of the phrase "punk rock" in print. "Ed Sanders, the founder of a New York-based weirdo band called The Fugs, had released a solo album called Sanders Truck Stop. And in this interview, he described his record as punk rock redneck sentimentality."

xref.title: Formation and Style (1973)
xref.body: Formed in 1973 in Rockford, Illinois, Cheap Trick were initially known for big hooks, similar to The Razberries, but their sound, largely due to guitarist Rick Nielsen, was more muscular, louder, and slightly more aggressive. They began by playing in various small venues like pubs and bowling alleys. "Cheap trick was formed in 1973 in Rockford, Illinois, a place just west of Chicago."

xref.title: Mental Health Struggles and Suicide Attempts (1993-2016)
xref.body: Sinead's mental health issues were public, including a denied suicide attempt involving sleeping pills in late 1993, and a definite attempt on her 33rd birthday (December 8, 1999) where she took 20 Valium pills following a custody court case involving her daughter Róisín. She was initially misdiagnosed with bipolar disorder, later receiving diagnoses of complex post-traumatic stress disorder and borderline personality disorder. In 2016, she disappeared from her Chicago suburb residence amidst rumors of a suicide attempt, but was located safely. "There was definitely a suicide attempt under 33rd birthday, which was December 8, 1999."

xref.title: Heathrow Airport Incident (August 25, 1996)
xref.body: Just two days after the MTV Unplugged event, on August 25, 1996, while Oasis was about to depart for another North American tour from Heathrow Airport, Liam, after boarding the plane while on the phone with his wife Patsy Kensit, suddenly announced he couldn't go and left the plane, stating he needed to "go buy a house." This resulted in the cancellation of their first major North American headlining gig at the 16,000-seat Rosemont Horizon in Chicago. "Suddenly, he says, can't go, gotta go buy a house."

xref.title: Final Concert at The Metro (2000)
xref.body: The Smashing Pumpkins' final show was announced on October 17, 2000, and took place on December 2nd at The Metro in Chicago. This club held significant history for the band, as it was also the venue where they played their first proper gig on October 5, 1988. The farewell performance was an emotional night that lasted four long hours, serving as a "grand finale" to their career.

xref.title: Chicago River Raw Sewage Incident – August 8, 2004, Kinzie Street Bridge, 800 lbs of Waste onto Tourist Boat
xref.body: At 1:18 pm on August 8, 2004, a Dave Matthews Band tour bus driven by Stephen Wooll crossed the Kinzie Street Bridge in Chicago — a metal grate structure over the Chicago River. Wooll took the opportunity to empty the bus's septic system through the grate. Directly beneath the bridge at that moment was the sightseeing boat *Little Lady*, loaded with approximately 100 tourists looking up at the Chicago skyline. Security cameras on the bridge captured the entire incident. Wooll was sentenced to 18 months probation, 150 hours of community service, and fined $10,000; a $70,000 lawsuit followed for violation of environmental laws. Dave Matthews and the band cooperated fully with the investigation, offering DNA samples to positively identify the waste, and donated $50,000 to Friends of the Chicago River. "800 pounds of human waste... there was a sightseeing boat called the Little Lady."

xref.title: "A Story Like Mine" – Spoken Word Performance (2018)
xref.body: At the Women's March in New York City in March 2018, Halsey performed a powerful spoken word piece that recounted deeply personal and traumatic experiences of sexual assault and abuse from various stages of her life, and that of her friends, tying it into the broader #MeToo movement. She described a friend's rape at 14 in 2009, her own childhood experience in 2002 by a neighbor's son, a coercive relationship in 2012, and a later assault in 2017 despite believing she was "protected" by her fame. She also revealed performing a show in Chicago while having a miscarriage. The piece emphasized that "nobody is safe" as long as women are alive and acknowledged figures like Ashley, Simone, Gabby, Makayla, Gaga, and Rosario Alli as heroes. "It's Halsey. We're siding up home from a women's march in New York City in March 2018."

xref.title: December 2021 Health Scare
xref.body: On December 9, 2021, the Foo Fighters' private jet was bound for Chicago to connect to a flight for Abu Dhabi, where they were scheduled to play the Formula One race season finale. However, a band member, believed to be Taylor Hawkins, had to be rushed to the hospital upon landing in Chicago, allegedly due to exhaustion and dehydration, which was unconfirmed by the band. This incident caused the band to miss their Abu Dhabi connection. "When the private jet landed in Chicago, a member of the band had to be rushed to hospital. We know this to be true, and that member seems to have been tailor."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Blackie O'Nassis Death (June 13, 2023) – Drummer on Pulp Fiction's "Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon"; Age 57, Cause Unknown
xref.body: John Rowan, who played under the name Blackie O'Nassis, was the drummer for Urge Overkill — the Chicago band whose cover of Neil Diamond's "Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon" (1967) appears in the famous dance scene in *Pulp Fiction*. The band was also a cult favorite in the alt-rock community and opened for Nirvana on the *Nevermind* tour, during which they befriended Kurt Cobain, Chrissie Hynde of the Pretenders, and Liz Phair. Blackie left the band in 1996; there were reports of heroin use and at least one arrest. The cause of his death on June 13, 2023, at age 57 was never disclosed. "As for the cause of his death on June 13th, 2023, we have no idea."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "Meek Technopop Ways" Epiphany
xref.body: Al Jourgensen experienced a transformative moment at a Front 242 concert in Chicago, which is said to have revealed the "error of his meek, techno pop ways" and catalyzed his band's shift towards a more aggressive industrial sound. "But legend has it that it was at a Front II-IV II show in Chicago that Alan Durgensen had as epiphany, of sorts, the one that showed him the error of his meek, techno pop ways."

xref.title: Albert Hammond Jr.'s Background and Role
xref.body: Albert Hammond Jr. is the son of Albert Hammond Sr., a successful songwriter who wrote songs for artists like Celine Dion, Aretha Franklin, Whitney Houston, Willie Nelson, Chicago, and The Carpenters, and had a writing credit on Radiohead's "Creep." In the early days of The Strokes, Albert was the band's business guy, booking gigs and pitching record companies under the pseudonym "Paul Spencer" (from his fake ID). He collected rejection letters by posting them on a wall. Crucially, he had a credit card funded by his father, which paid for essential band expenses like guitar strings, cables, drumsticks, and rehearsal PA. "Albert was the business guy of the band in the early days. He was the guy who booked gigs and pitch record companies, usually under the pseudonym Paul Spencer, which was the name he used on his old fake ID."

xref.title: Background and Mental Health
xref.body: Wesley Willis was a 6'5", 350 lb street artist from Chicago who began showing signs of schizophrenia in 1989, leading to institutionalization. He had distinctive behaviors, including head-butting as a greeting (resulting in a perpetual forehead bruise), and struggled with hygiene and unexpected vomiting, yet found solace in music. "Wesley was a 6'5, 350 lb street artist from Chicago. His thing was selling landscape drawings to people who passed by on the street."

xref.body: D'Arcy Elizabeth Wretzky met Billy Corgan and guitarist James Iha outside a club in Chicago in 1988 and "muscled her way into the new group, which would later become known as the smashing pumpkins." "The hardcore pumpkins fans were remembered that Darcy Elizabeth Retsky met Billy Corgan and guitarist James Eha outside of club in Chicago in 1988. And she sort of muscled her way into the new group, which would later become known as the smashing pumpkins."

xref.title: Bedroom Recordings as Girly Sound (Early 1990s)
xref.body: In Chicago, Liz Phair was part of the burgeoning low-fidelity scene by making cassettes of her songs in her bedroom under the name Girly Sound. This practice of recording in an intimate, home setting on basic equipment was a hallmark of the lo-fi movement, prioritizing raw artistic expression. "In Chicago, a woman named Liz Fair was making cassettes of her songs in her bedroom using the name Gurley Sound."

xref.title: Brad Wilk's Background and Influences
xref.body: Brad Wilk, originally from Chicago, started out as a guitarist before becoming a fan of The Who's drummer, Keith Moon. He pursued jazz drumming lessons from serious pros, idolizing Elvin Jones, from whom he learned funky grooves. He also studied James Brown and George Clinton records, mastering the technique of inserting a microsecond delay into his timekeeping, crucial for a good groove. "He also studied James Brown and George Clinton records and learned how to insert a microsecond delay into his time keeping something that's essential to a good groove."

xref.body: In December 2021, the Foo Fighters cancelled a scheduled gig after the Formula One race in Abu Dhabi because a band member (later suggested to be Taylor) had a medical emergency requiring transfer to a Chicago hospital while awaiting a commercial flight. "And now let's go back to December 2021. The food fighters were scheduled to play a gig after the final Formula One race in Abu Dhabi. But they never made it. We heard much later that a member of the band had a medical emergency and had to be transferred to the hospital in Chicago where the band was scheduled to take a commercial flight to the Middle East. That band member apparently was Taylor."

He appeared in at least five department store catalogs modeling back-to-school clothing for five-year-olds. His TV commercial work included spots for Hallmark greeting cards and Chuckles candy. "He would rather not be known as the cute child model for Bloomingdale's."

xref.title: Commercialization of the Fuzz Pedal
xref.body: After hearing the distinctive fuzzy guitar sound on Marty Robbins' "Don't Worry," Gibson Guitars approached Grady Martin to develop a commercial product. Martin, along with Glenn Snottie and Revis Hobbs, designed the circuit, and Gibson manufactured the first-ever fuzz pedal, the Maestro FZ1 Fuzz tone. This product made distortion widely available to guitarists. "When the prototype was ready, Grady and Glenn Snottie took the contraption, which had taken on the form of a foot pedal, to Gibson's offices in Chicago. They took one listen and said, this is brilliant. We'll take it."

xref.title: Cousin Tracy's Influence
xref.body: At age 13, Dave Grohl visited his cousin Tracy in Chicago, who had recently become a punk rocker. She took him to see a punk band at a small, dingy club called The Cubby Bear, across from Wrigley Field. This experience, filled with raw energy and loud music, completely changed his life and redirected his musical aspirations from being a "guitar virtuoso God" on a poster to being a part of a dynamic, accessible punk band. "my cousin Tracy had just turned into a punk rocker and she said, hey, I'm going out tonight. Do you want to see a band?"

xref.title: D'Arcy Wretzky's Post-Band Activities
xref.body: The story circulated that D'Arcy quit The Smashing Pumpkins in 1999 to pursue an acting career, though nothing seems to have come of those aspirations. On January 25, 2000, she was arrested on crack cocaine charges in Chicago, found with three bags of crack. She was not formally charged but received a court-ordered drug rehab program. Originally from Michigan, she is believed to be living on her horse farm near Watervillet, Michigan, east of Kalamazoo, where she raises Arabian horses. She also owns three antique shops and is reportedly a trained massage therapist. "The story was that in 1999 Darcy quit the pumpkins to pursue a career in acting. The following year, January 25, 2000, she was busted on crack cocaine charges. Cops on the west side of Chicago found her holding three bags of crack after the car in which she was a passenger made a couple of dumb and illegal uterines. Darcy was arrested but not formally charged. Instead, she received a court ordered drug rehab program."

xref.title: Early Label Deal and TVT Dispute
xref.body: Nine Inch Nails' first record deal was with TV Toons, a Chicago label previously specializing in TV theme song compilations, whose president, Steve Gottlieb, rebranded it as TVT. Gottlieb initially expected an "edgier Depeche Mode" but was deeply disappointed by "Pretty Hate Machine," calling it an "abortion" and predicting only 20,000 sales. This led to a "nightmare" legal battle lasting almost two years (1990-1992), during which Trent was contractually prohibited from releasing new music. "However, Trent was beginning to move beyond his favorite techno pop bands and into something a little more sinister and a lot harder."

xref.body: Joining Scream provided Dave Grohl with his first opportunities to tour extensively across America and, for the first time, in Europe (including Amsterdam), at ages 17 and 18, which he viewed as a liberating experience. xref.title: First Musician Shot – Chicago Dance Hall
xref.body: Pinedop Smith, a Boogie-Woogie piano player from Chicago, was the first musician known to have been shot. In 1929, just as he was about to enter a recording session, he was fatally shot during a fight at a dance hall. It is speculated that he might not have been the intended victim of the shooting. "He might not have been the intended victim, but he died all the same."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: First Professional Radio DJ
xref.body: Jack L. Cooper, a Black former boxer and semi-pro baseball player, became the host of "The All Negro Hour" on WBSC in Chicago, first broadcast on November 3rd, 1929. As his show grew in popularity, expanding to nine and a half hours a week by mid-1936, Cooper potentially became the first ever professional radio DJ by playing his personal collection of jazz and gospel records on air using his own phonograph. "He brought in his phonograph and collection of jazz and gospel records, which Cooper played on the air, and this would make Cooper the first ever professional radio DJ."

xref.title: First Touring Experiences (Scream)
xref.body: Touring America and Europe (including Amsterdam) with Scream at age 17 or 18 marked his first significant travels beyond Chicago. He cherished these experiences, seeing them as freedom and a clear path to his musical passion, despite the lack of money or large audiences. "And then to Europe for the first time. And wow, I'm an Amsterdam, and I'm 18, and I'm free, man. It was cool. It was great."

xref.body: Albert Hammond Sr. is a successful songwriter who wrote numerous songs for a wide array of prominent artists. He also received a writing credit on Radiohead's song "Creep" due to its melodic resemblance to "The Air That I Breathe," a song he wrote for The Hollies in the 1970s, as determined by a court case. xref.title: Vietnam Draft Evasion
xref.body: James Osterberg dodged the Vietnam War draft by convincing the draft board that he was gay. Following this, he attempted a career as a blues musician in Chicago before returning to Detroit. "After dodging the Vietnam draft by convincing the draft board that he was gay, James tried as hand at being a blues musician in Chicago before moving back to Detroit."
